name: IT Disaster Recovery Checklist
description: An IT disaster recovery checklist for small and mid-sized teams: priorities, backups, runbooks, incident response, recovery and testing.

items.text: List every critical system, application and data store
Map which business processes depend on each system
Set a recovery time objective (RTO) for each system
Set a recovery point objective (RPO) for each system
items.note: The RPO sets your backup frequency: a one-hour RPO needs at least hourly backups or replication.

items.text: Rank systems into recovery tiers, with dependencies first
items.note: Identity, DNS and networking usually have to come back before the applications that rely on them.

items.text: Get management sign-off on the targets and the budget they need
Follow the 3-2-1 rule: three copies, two media types, one off-site
Keep at least one immutable or offline backup copy
items.note: Ransomware commonly targets connected backups first, so an offline or immutable copy is your last line of defense.

items.text: Back up cloud and SaaS data, not just on-premises servers
Encrypt backups and store the keys separately
Use separate credentials with MFA for backup administration
Monitor backup jobs and alert on failures
Choose a recovery site: cloud, secondary data center or hot, warm or cold standby
Document network, firewall and DNS settings needed to fail over
Keep spare hardware or a replacement plan for key devices
Store licenses, installers and configuration exports off-site
Write step-by-step recovery runbooks for each tier-one system
Assign a recovery owner and a backup person for each system
Keep a contact list for staff, vendors, ISP, insurer and cloud providers
Store the plan where you can reach it if your systems are down
items.note: Keep a printed copy and a copy outside your own network, since the plan is useless if it lives only on the systems that failed.

items.text: Prepare message templates for staff and customers
Declare the incident and name an incident lead
Contain the problem: isolate infected or failing systems
Preserve logs and evidence before wiping anything in a security incident
Notify management, insurers and any regulators that require it
Log every decision and action with a timestamp
Restore systems in tier order, starting with dependencies
Check restored data is complete and from a clean point in time
Have system owners confirm each service works before go-live
Reset passwords and keys if credentials may be compromised
Watch restored systems closely for errors or reinfection
Run a test restore of sample files every month
Run a full disaster recovery test or tabletop exercise every year
Measure actual recovery times against your RTO and RPO
Hold a lessons-learned review after every test or real incident
Update the plan after major system, staff or vendor changes

faq.q: What is the difference between RTO and RPO?
faq.a: The recovery time objective (RTO) is how long a system can be down before the impact is unacceptable. The recovery point objective (RPO) is how much data, measured in time, you can afford to lose. A four-hour RPO means backups must run at least every four hours.

Keep at least three copies of your data, on two different types of storage, with one copy off-site. Many teams now add an immutable or offline copy as well, because ransomware often tries to delete or encrypt connected backups first.

faq.q: How is disaster recovery different from business continuity?
faq.a: Disaster recovery focuses on restoring IT systems and data. Business continuity is the wider plan for keeping the whole organisation running, including staff, premises, suppliers and customer communication. A disaster recovery plan is one part of business continuity.

faq.q: How often should a disaster recovery plan be tested?
faq.a: Test at least once a year and after any major change, such as a new system, a cloud migration or a change of backup provider. Restore individual files more often, for example monthly, to confirm backups are actually usable.
